data.title: 賴清德總統談關稅談判
data.transcript_raw: Actually, we know that the tariff war  has been going on for nearly a year now . One of the main reasons Trump started  the tariff war was the issue of trade  deficits. >> Now, a year later, have you noticed  that Taiwan's trade surplus with the  U.S. has hit a record high? >> We are worried that, indeed, while we  have already made sufficient investment  commitments in the past, we are  concerned that you might seize on the  data and continue to make more demands.  Are the tariff negotiations between the  Taiwan government and the U.S. side  still ongoing? What kind of bottom line  do we have to ensure our position? Some  countries might think this way: "He  only has two years left in his term,  maybe the midterm elections or the  presidential race will change things,"  so we can just drag it out, and maybe  after two years, nothing will happen.  How should we view the negotiation  approach that best serves the interests  of the Taiwan government? >> Yes, well, thank you, Ting-hao, for  bringing this up. It is very important.  Our tariff negotiations with the U.S.  are indeed driven by the fact that  Taiwan's trade surplus with the U.S. is  too large. There is already an estimate  for this year that Taiwan's total  export value will be around 900 billion  U.S. dollars. >> The largest destination for these  exports is likely the United States, so  it can be expected that Taiwan's trade  surplus with the U.S. this year. Will  be even higher than when he proposed  reciprocal tariffs last year. >> However, we uphold the stance of mutual  benefit; we do not speculate on how  much time he has left in his term, nor  do we think we can just drag it out and  be done with it. >> I believe that while these U.S.  reciprocal tariffs certainly pose a  challenge for Taiwan, they are also an  opportunity for Taiwan to further  integrate with the U.S. industrial  structure. Hmm. >> This is the mindset we hold. >> Many people think this might be a  crisis, but you believe it is actually  an opportunity. >> I think this is an opportunity. >> Because you have to see the development  of Taiwan's industry; in the past, we  moved West. >> Hmm. >> Then we moved South. Later, we moved  North, cooperating with Japan, and now  we should move East across the Pacific  to join with the U.S. >> It is time for further integration; in  the history of our industry, the time  to head in this direction has arrived. >> It just so happens that this provided  an opportunity, and our negotiations  this time have truly upheld a position  of mutual benefit. >> Hmm. >> Meaning we invest in the U.S. And they  will also come to Taiwan to invest. >> That is, Taiwan has a "national team"  investing in the U.S., and the U.S. has  a "national team" investing in Taiwan.  This is true for the tech industry, the  defense industry, as well as other  sectors. >> So, under these conditions of mutual  benefit, the U.S. also sees Taiwan's  strength. And sees the necessity of  Taiwan's industry to U.S. development. >> And its importance. >> It also shows that the various policies  proposed by the Taiwan government are  solid.
